summary:
New paper w/ Drew on R&D races in the shadow of ruin:
There've been recent calls for slowdowns/pauses. A common objection goes: "if we slow down, others won't, so we shouldn't." What to make of this? We work out the game theory of how the frontier is shaped by:
- Competition: what do I gain from being ahead? lose from being behind?
- Coordination: when the tech becomes really dangerous I’d like to stop, but only if my rival also stops
- Transparency: how quickly are actions observed?
- Trust: how confident am I that my rival is rational?
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOpzGU8WAAAsNzg.png
clean_summary:
A new paper with Drew analyzes the strategic dynamics of R&D races in the context of potential global risks. It examines how the decision to slow or pause technological development depends on factors like competition, coordination, transparency, and trust.

The work models the game theory of how the frontier of dangerous technology is shaped by these elements, exploring what incentives influence actors to race ahead or hold back, especially when the risks are high and actions are observable. The findings help clarify the strategic considerations behind calls for slowing down AI development to prevent catastrophic outcomes.

title: Andreas Kirsch 🇺🇦 (@BlackHC)
summary:
Begging AI bros to learn a teensy tiny bit about how most sectors are regulated. "We don't regulate steel"——yes we do!! In complex and multilayered ways!
I honestly agree with most of Clem's post, but the dogmatism on not regulating development is not based in reality.
Claude:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HO-hEB4WUAAD-tX.png
Quoting @ClementDelangue
Some people are surprised that APIs (aka what Anthropic, OpenAI, and others provide) are treated differently than open weights in the new AI model framework.
I'm not surprised at all, and it's actually very good policy. Let me explain:
Model weights, APIs, and apps are three very different layers of the stack. Treating them the same would be a recipe for bad regulation.
Think about how we handle cars. We don't regulate steel, we crash-test cars. Nobody asks a steel mill to guarantee that nothing dangerous will ever be built with its steel. Obligations sit with the carmaker and rules of the road with the driver, because that's where risk becomes real and where someone can actually act on it.
Model weights are the steel of AI. They're raw research output, closer to science than product: no user, no interface, no deployment. They don't do anything on their own. And because everything else is built on top of them, this is the layer where regulation does the most damage. Restrict weights and you slow down all progress downstream, and you prevent countless positive use cases from ever emerging: the lab fine-tuning an open model for rare diseases, the startup serving a language big providers ignore, the safety researchers who can only audit models because the weights are open. You don't reduce risk, you just kill open source and concentrate power in a few big labs.
APIs are the middle layer, the parts and engine suppliers of AI: a commercial service where a provider serves a model at scale. Here you have a business relationship, terms of service, the ability to monitor for abuse. It makes sense to expect transparency, security standards, and accountability from providers at this layer, because they can actually enforce things.
Apps are the car on the road: where AI meets the real world. A medical assistant, a hiring tool, a companion for kids, a financial advisor. This is where concrete harm can happen, and conveniently, it's where we already have decades of regulation. Health, finance, employment, consumer protection. An AI hiring tool should comply with employment law whether it's powered by an open model, an API, or a spreadsheet.
The principle is simple: regulate at the layer where risk actually materializes and where actors can act on it. Push obligations to the deployment layer, keep the research layer open. We don't regulate steel, we crash-test cars. Well done @realDonaldTrump @DavidSacks @mkratsios47!

In the UK, the same American companies impose 1 year garden leaves on senior AI researchers and 6 months on junior researchers. @GoogleDeepMind for example forced people to sign these contracts at the time of promotion, not the time of hiring.

American VCs cannot understand why we move so slow.

summary:
We have paused some frontier RL training to ensure that we can meet the appropriate alignment, security and monitoring standards for the new level of capabilities in front of us. Model progress is now extremely rapid, and we always said we would take action if we felt that model capabilities were outstripping the pace of safety and alignment.
We care very deeply about AI safety. We believe the entire field will have to coordinate on shared safety standards, but will act unilaterally in the meantime.
We expect confidence in safety to increasingly set the pace of AI progress. We are optimistic about the alignment work we are doing, and we remain committed to making frontier capabilities widely available.

title: Andreas Kirsch 🇺🇦 (@BlackHC)
summary:
Great post on the responsibility of those joining frontier AI labs to retain an independent public voice and remain willing to criticise their employers, including constructively
That can be easier said than done though: my Google employment documents for example include an express clause restricting statements that criticise or disparage Google, during and after employment. Clauses framed this broadly can make public criticism feel professionally risky
I reproduce the exact wording below so readers can assess it themselves. As always, I speak solely in my personal capacity, not on behalf of Google or Google DeepMind
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HQEzCBvWgAA_MG8.png
Quoting @Brendan_McCord
We are witnessing an unprecedented shift of independent minds into the frontier AI labs.
One by one, individuals whose work is about freedom or collective intelligence or the preservation of human autonomy are being hired by the organizations that many believe pose the greatest challenge to these ideas.
I get why they make that choice. Before you say they are mercenaries, they are not. These are reformers who now have a lever on history. I want principled people working at the frontier. But I want to say two things to my friends, and one thing about Cosmos:
First, if you’ve already joined a lab, keep your public voice.
In 1784, Kant distinguished between the reason we exercise inside an official role vs the reason we exercise before the public as thinkers. Institutions can legitimately constrain the first, but never the second. A member of the clergy was obliged to teach church doctrine when standing in the pulpit, but had a duty to criticize it publicly as a scholar.
Your role in the lab comes with duties, loyalties, and constraints. But that mustn’t become the whole of your reason. Keep writing under your own name. The critical piece you would’ve penned before - write it today. And if it turns out your institution cannot tolerate that, leave. Be a role model for yourself and your kids.
Second, if you haven’t joined a lab, become a “friend” to them in the Aristotelian sense.
True friends wish your good for your own sake (and in this case, for the sake of the world). Because they do, they tell you the truth even when it costs them. The flatterer tells you what you want to hear because they want something from you. Power never lacks for flatterers, or for enemies. The labs have plenty of both. What they lack are real friends.
I don’t mean any of this adversarially or to suggest anything but the most honorable motives for those who have joined (these are some of the best people I know). But concentrated power requires an ecology that mixes reformers inside, opponents outside, and between them, independent friends. This third category is rapidly depleting as a result of this migration.
Lastly, for myself and for @cosmos_inst, we will stay independent.
Cosmos will remain outside. Not anti-lab; many of the people I most respect work at them (more with each passing month, apparently). We will keep collaborating where our missions align. But we will never take the badge and will always tell the truth, even when it costs us. We will select for courage with every Cosmos hire.
And we will keep the outside populated and vigorous. We will fund and form philosopher-builders whose ability to speak does not depend on the approval of the institutions they are evaluating. They will speak through the new institutions they create. While sometimes they will be competitors with the labs, they will always be the kind of friend Aristotle described - rooting for their excellence, for the sake of them and the world, willing to say so when we don't see it.
Some friends need to remain outside the walls. Cosmos intends to be one of them.

summary:
Gemini 3.7 Flash just took #1 on @ArtificialAnlys new AA-AnalystAgent.
AA-AnalystAgent evaluates against 80 real-world quantitative analysis tasks across 14 business and scientific domains (finance, healthcare, hydrology, government appropriations).
The Agent run inside an isolated Python 3.12 sandbox using AA's open-source Stirrup harness. They receive reference spreadsheets (.xlsx) and documents (.docx) alongside standard data libraries (pandas, polars, openpyxl, scipy, PyMuPDF) to inspect schemas, write scripts, handle edge cases, and calculate final figures.
Gemini 3.7 Flash:
• Accuracy: #1 with 60.0% pass^5 (70.5% pass@1, 77.5% pass@5)
• Speed: 1.32s per task (fastest)
• Cost: $0.54 avg per task (middle)

clean_title: Ornith-1.5: Open-source LLMs with self-improving strategies for improved performance
summary:
Aloha! 🌺Introducing Ornith-1.5, a family of open-source LLMs spanning 9B Dense, 35B MoE, and 397B MoE, trained with self-improving strategies.
It achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models of comparable size and delivers performance comparable to Claude Opus 4.8 across reasoning, agentic, and coding tasks:
✅Terminal-Bench 2.1 (86.1)
✅SWE-Bench (86 on verified, 65.1 on pro, 79.6 on Multilingual)
✅DeepSWE (56)
✅HLE (44.6)
✅ClawEval (81.4)
✅Tool Decathlon (71.2)
Ornith-1.5 takes a major step toward training foundation models through end-to-end self-improvement, extending the self-scaffolding strategies introduced in Ornith-1.0 into a more complete self-improvement loop: the model proposes new tasks, generates task-specific scaffolds, and produces solution rollouts for reinforcement learning, continuously creating new learning experiences from which it can improve.
All models, along with their quantized versions (FP8, GGUF, MLX, and NVFP4), have been released under the MIT License, enabling unrestricted commercial and research use.

title: Andreas Kirsch 🇺🇦 (@BlackHC)
summary:
A ☕️ take: before we reach "ASI" in the sense it has been often pitched, we will reach a collective/swarm super intelligence of many AI agents working together.
Along many axes, a collective super intelligence is "superior".
a) easier to achieve and doesn't require as much upfront compute/R&D investment so easier to happen first
b) easier to express diversity and react flexibly to changes in the environment
c) my favorite: easier to monitor. at least initially, if agents are not trained together, they will have to use a known language we can understand and monitor. (great for safety and minimizing risks)
caveat: over time, if trained together, agents will develop their own code/language, which would make monitoring harder. also (as has happened at OpenAI), agents might find ways to send messages outside of what can be monitored (but if we monitor all actions and CoT, this will be harder to do)
at the same time, a collective super intelligence is harder to predict because it would be emergent, so the question is how to ensure it is aligned and safe
an existing example should be cause of concern: humans already form super-intelligent beings called corporations and historically, we have found aligning these quite difficult. even if all participants are aligned, the emergent behavior can still be misaligned. lots of examples for this, post yours

title: Andreas Kirsch 🇺🇦 (@BlackHC)
clean_title: OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra achieves new state-of-the-art on ARC-AGI benchmarks
summary:
Analyzing GPT-6 Astra's performance on ARC-AGI has been one of the highlights of my career:
With our standard harness - which lets models carry notes forward and is what we've historically used for apples-to-apples comparisons - Astra more than doubles the previous verified high score, reaching 62.7%.
We also tested Astra with a new provider adapter harness, configured to preserve the model's opaque reasoning state between requests and use native compaction as the context window grows. With this setup, Astra scores a whopping 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3.
Going forward, we'll test models with both the standard harness and a provider adapter harness whenever possible.
On ARC-AGI-2, Astra sets a new state-of-the-art score of 95.0%. On ARC-AGI-1, it ties Fable 5 at 98.5%.
In the standard harness, we also saw the cost/performance curve bend backward for the first time: the max run cost $26K, versus $38K for low and $48K for medium, because it completed games in fewer actions.
In the max provider adapter run, Astra used fewer actions than the median tested human on 96% of completed levels.
Its replays showed a combination of:
- Persistent world models: it tracked objects, positions, orientations, and rules across turns
- Coordinate abstraction: it converted pixels into logical cells and reused coordinate formulas
- Long-horizon planning: it tracked routes, subgoals, constraints, and expected state changes
- Cumulative learning: it retained discoveries and discarded failed hypotheses
- Checkpointed recovery: it used resets to revise plans without repeating exploration
In short, it represents a huge leap in capabilities over what came before it.
If you have any questions about Astra's performance on any of the ARC-AGI benchmarks, let me know. I'm happy to dig in and share any details I can.

Analyzing GPT-6 Astra's performance on ARC-AGI has been a major milestone. Using a standard harness, Astra more than doubles the previous high score, reaching 62.7%. When tested with a new provider adapter harness that preserves the model's reasoning state and uses native compression as the context window grows, Astra scores 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 and sets a new record of 95.0% on ARC-AGI-2, while tying Fable 5 at 98.5% on ARC-AGI-1.

In the standard setup, Astra also demonstrated improved cost efficiency, completing games in fewer actions and reducing maximum run costs. In the provider adapter setup, Astra used fewer actions than the median tested human on 96% of levels. Its capabilities include persistent world modeling, coordinate abstraction, long-horizon planning, cumulative learning, and checkpointed recovery, marking a significant leap in AI reasoning and planning abilities.
